item.title: Impact of technologies on dairy farms
item.description:
For this project, I am looking for Master’s (M.Sc.) and/or Ph.D. students in veterinary sciences. If you’re interested in the use of technologies on dairy farms and want to explore their impact on animal health and farmers’ quality of life, feel free to contact me here!

Team

  • José Denis-Robichaud (principal investigator)
  • Geneviève Brisson (UQAR, collaborator)
  • Stephen LeBlanc (University of Guelph, collaborator)

In brief

Various technologies are used on dairy farms to support management, improve productivity and herd health, and reduce the workload of dairy producers. This “smart farming” is rapidly expanding, and the range of technologies available to dairy producers is extensive. Overall, the goal of this project is to address on-farm technologies by considering the interconnection between cow and farmer health (One Health approach). For this project, we will develop and launch a Canadian survey assessing the use of technologies on dairy farms, cow reproduction and health, and the professional quality of life of dairy producers. We will then conduct a qualitative study in Québec exploring the use of different technological tools and the challenges associated with them. In a context where responsible innovation is increasingly demanded, the results of these studies will help us understand the impact of smart farming on various aspects of health. Moreover, the insights from producers gathered through this project will help guide the use of data generated by these technologies to develop machine learning models that support decision-making related to fertility and health in dairy cows.

Funding

This project is made possible through the support of the Fondation Agria.

item.title: Use of bacterial markers to predict endometritis in dairy cows
item.description:
This project needs a Master’s degree (M.Sc.) student in veterinary science. If you have a background in veterinary medicine, animal science, molecular biology, bioinformatics, or a related field, and you have experience in research laboratories and working with cattle, please contact us!

This study aims to detect bacterial markers present in the uterus of dairy cows that can predict the onset of endometritis.

Team

  • Marcio Costa (principal investigator)
  • Hélène Lardé (collaborator)
  • Isabella Nicola (collaborator)
  • José Denis-Robichaud (collaborator)

In brief

Endometritis, an inflammation of the inner lining of the uterus, is common in dairy cows, particularly in the postpartum period. It affects fertility and overall health, resulting in significant economic losses in the dairy industry. The significant consequences of endometritis include longer intervals between pregnancies, increased need for veterinary care, and use of antimicrobials, which are associated with decreased performance. Nearly 100% of cows have bacterial contamination in the uterus after calving, and expected changes in the microbiota are observed during uterine involution. However, when there are imbalances in the resident bacteria, the environment becomes more susceptible to the proliferation of pathogenic organisms, such as Trueperella and E. coli. New DNA sequencing and quantification technologies have become readily available in recent decades, enabling exponential growth in our understanding of the relationship between the host and its microbiota. Therefore, this study aims to detect bacterial markers present in the uterus of dairy cows that can predict the onset of endometritis.

Funding

MAPAQ/Ministère de l’Agriculture, des Pêcheries et de l’Alimentation
Innovation bioalimentaire - Volet 2: Recherche appliquée, développement expérimental et adaptation technologique
